newsitem.title: LEBANON: Japanese envoy in Syria for talks on Red Army.
newsitem.headline: Japanese envoy in Syria for talks on Red Army.

text.p: A Japanese envoy arrived in Damascus on Tuesday for talks with Syrian officials on the fate of five people arrested in Lebanon and suspected of being members of the Japanese Red Army guerrilla group.
Hiroshi Hirabayashi, chief foreign policy adviser for Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, told reporters on arrival he would convey a message to President Hafez al-Assad from the Japanese premier.
Syria is the main foreign power broker in Lebanon where it has some 35,000 troops. The five Red Army suspects were arrested last month along with other Asians in Lebanon.
"I am carrying a message to President Hafez al-Assad from Prime Minister Hashimoto. I would like to discuss bilateral relations and the (Middle East) peace process," Hirabayashi said.
He said that "if time permits" he would like to discuss the issues that have come up in Lebanon.

The Japanese envoy, who arrived from Beirut after meetings there, said he was "very satisfied" with his talks in Lebanon with President Elias Hrawi, Prime Minister Rafik Hariri and other judicial officials on the case of the Red Army men.
The Red Army issue has been mired in confusion since Hashimoto said in Tokyo on February 18 that Lebanese officials had told him they had arrested six Japanese suspected members of the group.
Most Lebanese officials have since been tight-lipped or have made contradictory statements on whether any suspected members of the group are being held.
A high-ranking Lebanese judicial source said in Beirut earlier on Tuesday that Lebanon was holding five Japanese Red Army guerrillas in Beirut.

The source named the five alleged guerrillas as Kazua Tohira, 44, Hisashi Matsuda, 48, Mariko Yamamoto, 56, Masao Adachi, 57 and 49-year-old Kozo Okamoto. Okamoto was involved in the May 1972 shootout at Tel Aviv's Lod Airport in which 24 people died and 100 were injured.
Prosecutor General Adnan Addoum told reporters that a Japanese security delegation handed him documents identifying five out of eight Japanese citizens arrested as Red Army guerrillas.

The Red Army, founded in 1971, is allied to hardline anti-Israeli Palestinian factions. Lebanon's Bekaa Valley was a haven during Lebanon's 1975-90 civil war for a wide range of guerrilla groups, including Lebanese Islamists and Marxists, Palestinian factions, Kurds and the Red Army.
"We will open investigations to confirm their identity within 24 hours and if it proves that they have committed crimes in Lebanon, they will be tried here," Addoum told reporters.
On Monday, a Japanese envoy indicated that Tokyo no longer expected Lebanon to deport detained Red Army suspects immediately but still hoped for extradition after Lebanese justice runs its course.
Japan and Lebanon do not have an extradition agreement but Hirabayashi said they would study the extradition issue if it was confirmed that the suspects were Japanese members of the Red Army.
